meta.note: Three of six cited. Engine naming updated: AWS documents “Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS” — Redis is now explicitly “Redis OSS” following the licence change, and Valkey is listed first. Also new since this write-up: node-based Valkey clusters can enable durability via a Multi-AZ transactional log, which weakens the old “volatile by default” framing.

name: Amazon ElastiCache
oneLiner: Managed in-memory Redis/Memcached for microsecond caching and speed.
whatItIs: ElastiCache is AWS's managed in-memory data store, running Redis (now also the OSS fork Valkey) or Memcached. It keeps hot data in RAM so reads return in microseconds instead of the milliseconds a database takes. The classic use is a cache sitting in front of a slower store (RDS, DynamoDB): the app checks the cache first and only hits the database on a miss, cutting latency and load. Beyond caching, Redis on ElastiCache also serves as a fast store for sessions, rate-limiters, leaderboards, queues and pub/sub. It's an accelerator, not a system of record.

inPractice.narrative: A high-traffic app reads a user's profile constantly. Instead of querying RDS every time, it caches the profile in ElastiCache (Redis): the first read populates the cache, subsequent reads return in microseconds, and the database only sees a fraction of the traffic. On a write, the app updates RDS and invalidates the cache entry. ElastiCache sits between the app and the database as a speed layer — it holds a copy of hot data, not the source of truth.

coreConcepts.detail: Data lives in RAM, so reads/writes are sub-millisecond — orders of magnitude faster than disk-backed databases, at the cost of memory being finite and (by default) volatile.
Redis/Valkey offers rich data structures, persistence, replication and pub/sub; Memcached is a simpler, multi-threaded pure cache. Most new work picks Redis/Valkey.
The common design: app reads cache, on a miss loads from the DB and populates the cache, and invalidates/updates on writes. TTLs bound staleness.
Redis cluster mode shards data across nodes for scale; replicas provide read scaling and failover for availability.
When memory fills, an eviction policy (e.g. LRU) drops keys; TTLs expire entries. Getting these right controls hit rate and staleness.
ElastiCache Serverless removes node sizing, auto-scaling capacity to demand and billing by usage — simpler for variable workloads.

whenToUse: Caching hot data to cut database load and latency (cache-aside).
Session stores, rate limiting, leaderboards and counters.
Sub-millisecond reads that a disk-backed database can't hit.
Redis pub/sub or lightweight queues alongside caching.
Absorbing read spikes in front of RDS/DynamoDB.
whenNotToUse: As the system of record — it's volatile/finite memory, not durable primary storage.
Large datasets that don't fit (economically) in RAM.
Analytical queries and joins — that's a warehouse's job.
Data that must never be lost without careful persistence/replication design.

keyFacts.label: Type
keyFacts.value: Managed in-memory cache/store — Valkey, Memcached or Redis OSS.

source.quote: Amazon ElastiCache works with the Valkey, Memcached, and Redis OSS engines.

keyFacts.label: Scaling
keyFacts.value: Redis cluster-mode sharding + replicas; Serverless option.

source.quote: You can operate Amazon ElastiCache in two formats. You can get started with a serverless cache or create a node-based cluster. … ElastiCache Serverless is compatible with Valkey 7.2 and higher, Memcached 1.6.22 and above, and Redis OSS 7.1.

keyFacts.label: Role
keyFacts.value: Accelerator in front of a durable store, not the source of truth.

keyFacts.label: Durability
keyFacts.value: Volatile by default; Redis persistence/replication optional.

source.quote: For node-based Valkey clusters, you can enable durability to persist your data in a distributed Multi-AZ transactional log. With durability enabled, your data is protected even if all cache nodes fail.

keyFacts.label: Billing
keyFacts.value: Per node-hour (by memory/type) or Serverless per-usage.

pricingShape: Node-based ElastiCache bills per node-hour by instance type (which sets the RAM you get), plus replicas for HA/read scaling and some data transfer — so cost tracks how much memory you keep online, running continuously. Reserved nodes cut cost for steady use. ElastiCache Serverless instead bills by data stored and requests, auto-scaling capacity, which suits spiky or unpredictable workloads. The main levers are sizing memory to your hot set (not your whole dataset), a good eviction/TTL policy to keep hit rates high, and choosing node vs serverless by traffic shape.
gotchas: It's a cache, not a database — treat cached data as disposable and keep the durable copy elsewhere.
Cache invalidation is genuinely hard; stale data from missed invalidations causes subtle bugs.
Under-sized memory plus aggressive eviction tanks the hit rate, negating the benefit.
A cold cache after restart/failover briefly stampedes the database — plan for warm-up.
Redis persistence/replication must be configured deliberately if you need any durability.
